name: Anti-estrogen / AI for masculine look

lead: Aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole block the enzyme that makes oestrogen. Some looksmaxxing and bodybuilding users take them outside medical supervision for a leaner, drier, more masculine look, less water retention and breast tissue, and among younger users, a taller final height.

The chain is hormonal: aromatase converts testosterone and other androgens into oestrogens, so blocking it lowers circulating oestrogen, and oestrogen helps close growth plates, which is the basis of the height idea. The drugs are approved mainly for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer, with experimental work in delayed puberty and short stature and approval for precocious puberty in boys alongside other medicines. No trial has tested them for appearance in healthy men.

paras: Users discuss them mainly alongside testosterone or steroid use, to manage oestrogen, and some younger users discuss them for height.

Reported effects include joint pain, fatigue, hot flushes, bone loss, cardiovascular effects, and rare liver or skin reactions. They are prescription-only and contraindicated in pregnancy; buying them without a prescription is the grey market.

web.title: Anti-estrogen / AI for masculine look — Grokipedia

angle.text: Aromatase inhibitors lower oestrogen, which is meant to mean less water retention and breast tissue for a leaner, more masculine look, and a longer growth window for young users. They are approved for other medical uses; trials in healthy men for these goals are lacking.

lead: "AI" in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding slang usually means an aromatase inhibitor, a drug such as anastrozole (Arimidex), letrozole or exemestane that blocks the enzyme converting androgens into oestrogens. Users who take these drugs outside a medical indication describe goals such as a leaner, more masculine look, less water retention or breast tissue, controlling oestrogen alongside testosterone use, and, among younger users, taller final height.[1][2]

Aromatase inhibitors are approved mainly for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women; anastrozole was patented in 1987 and approved for medical use in 1995.[2] Large trials such as ATAC compared anastrozole with tamoxifen in breast cancer.[3] Wikipedia says use in men is off-label, with experimental work in delayed puberty and short stature, and that the drugs are approved for precocious puberty in boys when combined with other medicines.[1][2]

No published trial has tested aromatase inhibitors for improving the appearance of healthy men. Research on them in men concerns specific medical conditions, and documented adverse effects include joint pain, bone loss and cardiovascular effects.
infobox: Patented by ICI 1987; approved for medical use 1995; brand Arimidex[2]
Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer; peripheral precocious puberty in boys (with another drug)[1][2]

paras: Aromatase inhibitors lower oestrogen by blocking aromatase, the enzyme that converts androgens (testosterone and androstenedione) to oestrogens. Exemestane is steroidal and irreversible; anastrozole and letrozole are nonsteroidal and reversible.[1] Anastrozole has a half-life of about 40 to 50 hours and, in postmenopausal women, reduces circulating oestradiol by at least 85 percent.[2]
Fulvestrant, sometimes grouped in discussion of anti-oestrogens, is a different type: an oestrogen-receptor downregulator given by injection for breast cancer.

Wikipedia describes aromatase inhibitors as off-label substances used in so-called hardmaxxing to pursue greater height, a more masculine look and more muscle mass.[4] Forum posts include young users asking how to obtain anastrozole without a prescription in order to reach a taller height; this wiki does not reproduce sourcing or dosing information.

Proponents' reasoning is that oestrogen drives fat distribution, water retention and breast tissue in men, and that oestrogen promotes growth-plate closure so lowering it could extend growth. Wikipedia reports that aromatase inhibitors have been studied experimentally in idiopathic short stature, where slowing growth-plate fusion may give growth hormone more time to work.[1]

For gynecomastia, a 2023 paediatric review says it arises from an imbalance of androgen to oestrogen action along with other factors such as obesity and drugs. Wikipedia describes anastrozole as surprisingly ineffective for gynecomastia compared with tamoxifen, while noting that it raises testosterone in men.[2]
In breast cancer, the ATAC trial of 9,366 postmenopausal women found anastrozole prolonged disease-free survival compared with tamoxifen.[3] These results do not address appearance in healthy men.

Wikipedia lists common effects of anastrozole as hot flushes, fatigue, joint pain, hypertension, depression, nausea, rash, osteoporosis and fractures, with rarer skin reactions and abnormal liver tests.[2] A case report describes a lichenoid skin eruption associated with anastrozole.

Bone loss is a documented concern in women; Wikipedia says men do not appear to show the same bone effects but that long-term effects on bone mineral density remain a concern.[1][2] Reported effects in young people include slowed bone maturation.[1]

No studies found for the use of aromatase inhibitors to improve masculine appearance in healthy men. Clinical trials in the sources concern breast cancer, such as the ATAC trial comparing anastrozole with tamoxifen,[3] and the experimental use in short stature is described only as experimental.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and related forums, aromatase inhibitors come up in conversations about height, leanness and testosterone use, including among teenagers.[4]

claims.claim: Lowering oestrogen with an AI can add height in teenagers.
AIs give a leaner, more masculine look and control gynecomastia.
AIs are low-risk if used carefully.

timeline.event: Angela Brodie's work leads to first clinical trials of the aromatase inhibitor formestane.[1]
First results of the ATAC trial of anastrozole versus tamoxifen published.[5]
